analysis.one_liner: Imposes fees on tobacco companies that miss youth-smoking targets and gives the FDA power to regulate tobacco, while funding public health programs.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to three House committees in November 1997 and never received a committee vote or a floor vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required each tobacco manufacturer to cut the number of children smoking its brands by set percentages each year, with per-unit fees for companies that fell short, and allowed higher fees and eventually plain packaging for repeat offenders. It would have given the FDA full authority to regulate tobacco manufacturing, labeling, advertising, and ingredients. It also would have reimbursed states for treating tobacco-related illness, funded anti-smoking ads and quit programs, paid tobacco farmers to exit the business, and expanded Head Start and child care. It sat in three House committees and died there.
analysis.who_benefits: Children, who would face a regulated, fee-penalized industry actively measured on how many of them smoke; smokers who want to quit, through federally funded cessation programs; states, which would be reimbursed for treating tobacco-related illness; biomedical researchers and universities, which would get new grant funding; and tobacco farmers and their communities, who would receive buyout payments and economic-development grants to move away from tobacco.

how_it_helps.text: Requires every tobacco maker to reduce the number of children using its products on a declining schedule — to 60% of baseline by year four and 20% by year ten — with per-unit fees of 2 to 6 cents for missing the targets, escalating fees for consecutive failures, and a move to generic, logo-free packaging after four straight years of failure.

Gives the Food and Drug Administration explicit authority over tobacco for the first time, including ingredient disclosure, warning labels, advertising regulation, and performance standards that could reduce or eliminate nicotine and tar.

Reimburses states for money spent treating tobacco-related illness under Medicaid, with the federal share redirected to children's programs such as Head Start, child care, and children's health insurance if the state certifies that use.

Authorizes roughly $2.1 billion in the first year for counter-advertising, CDC anti-smoking programs, cessation research, FDA enforcement, and state block grants for tobacco-use reduction and education.

Creates a public National Tobacco Document Depository forcing manufacturers, the Tobacco Institute, and the Council for Tobacco Research to open their internal files on health research, addiction, and marketing to minors, with a panel of federal judges to resolve privilege disputes.

Pays tobacco quota owners to permanently give up their quotas and pays tobacco producers to stop growing quota tobacco, while funding economic-development block grants for tobacco-dependent communities.

analysis.who_pays: Tobacco manufacturers bear the noncompliance fees, FDA regulation, ingredient disclosure, and forced document disclosure; the bill expressly allows them to pass those fee costs on to consumers, so adult smokers would pay higher prices — which the bill treats as an intended deterrent. Taxpayers fund the farm buyout (about $9.2 billion over three years) and community grants.

drawbacks.text: The bill allows manufacturers to pass noncompliance fees on to consumers, so adult smokers — including low-income smokers — would pay more per pack, a cost the bill calls 'a further economic deterrent' but which falls on people legally using a legal product.

The buyout would pay quota owners and farmers roughly $9.2 billion in federal money to stop growing tobacco, transferring public funds to holders of a government-created license even if they were not actively farming.

The youth-use targets are set by surveying how many children use each brand — something a manufacturer cannot fully control — and courts could review the surveys only after the fees were paid, a design that invited years of fee-and-litigate rather than clean compliance.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public-health upside was large: over 400,000 deaths a year were attributed to tobacco, over 90% of smokers started as minors, and the government was spending over $20 billion a year treating tobacco-related illness. The main costs — higher cigarette prices passed to smokers and billions for a farm buyout — were deliberate: price increases deter youth smoking, and the buyout was the political price of ending the quota system. The bill was a sweeping, multi-committee proposal that in reality would have been heavily amended; as written, its benefits to children and public health plausibly outweighed its costs, though its enforcement design was clunky and the buyout generous to quota owners.

outcome.mechanism: It went to three House committees the day it was introduced, got divided among subcommittees, and no committee ever held a markup or voted on it, so it died when the Congress ended in January 1999.

narrative.text: DeLauro introduced the bill on November 12, 1997, and it was referred the same day to the Commerce, Education and the Workforce, and Agriculture Committees.
Within five weeks it was split among five subcommittees, including the Health and Environment Subcommittee of Commerce, and no further committee action of any kind appears in the record.
The bill attracted 31 cosponsors, 30 of them Democrats and one Republican, and no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever occurred before the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Tobacco manufacturers were better off: they avoided per-unit fees, FDA regulation of nicotine, forced disclosure of internal documents, and legally binding youth-smoking targets. Tobacco growers also lost out — the promised buyout and community transition grants never happened.

for.name: Rosa DeLauro
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on it twice, in November 1997 and April 1998.

for.name: 31 House cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Representatives Pallone, Lowey, Pelosi, DeGette, Miller, McGovern, Meehan, and Waters.

against.name: Tom Bliley
against.what_they_did: Received the referral of the bill on November 12, 1997, and never scheduled a markup or brought it to a committee vote.

against.name: Chairs of the House Agriculture and Education and the Workforce Committees
against.what_they_did: Received secondary referrals of the bill and took no action beyond subcommittee referrals; neither committee ever reported the bill.

against.name: Major tobacco manufacturers
against.role: Cigarette makers including Philip Morris, R.J. Reynolds, and Brown & Williamson
against.what_they_did: Opposed comprehensive tobacco legislation in the 105th Congress through an extensive lobbying and advertising campaign; their bill would have faced fees, FDA regulation, and forced disclosure of internal documents.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so there is no roll-call record; what support existed was almost entirely Democratic — 30 of 31 cosponsors were Democrats — while the Republican chairs of all three referred committees never moved the bill.

industries.note: The bill imposes per-unit fees tied to youth-smoking reduction targets, FDA authority over nicotine and ingredients, advertising limits, and mandatory public disclosure of internal documents on addiction and youth marketing. It allows companies to pass fee costs to consumers, making adult smokers pay part of the price.

Quota owners would be paid to permanently surrender their quotas and growers to stop raising tobacco — federal money to exit a declining, publicly subsidized market. The cost falls on taxpayers, but the payments came with economic-development grants for tobacco towns.

Universities, research hospitals, NIH, and NSF would receive new grant funding for basic and biomedical research plus fellowships and loan forgiveness for young scientists, funded from tobacco revenues.

industries.industry: Early childhood education and child care providers
industries.note: The bill directs large new funding to Head Start, Early Head Start, child care block grants, and after-school programs, expanding services for working families with young children.

industries.industry: Event and sports sponsorship (replacing tobacco sponsorship)
industries.note: The bill creates transitional sponsorship grants so athletic, musical, and cultural events formerly funded by tobacco companies can find substitute public funding instead.
